582.title: The pledge under the tree
582.hook: Allah was pleased with the believers when they pledged under the tree (48:18)
582.howItsDone: Many Muslims honor the Companions who pledged at Hudaybiyyah as the people of the tree, and the bay'ah, a pledge given by hand, remains a form of commitment in many communities and Sufi orders.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was sakinah, the stillness sent down, and your line was tranquillity comes down. Did one slow breath change a tense moment? Day five hundred eighty-two.

Rewind a few days before the treaty. The Prophet ﷺ has sent 'Uthman ibn 'Affan into Mecca as his envoy, to explain that the Muslims have come only as pilgrims. 'Uthman doesn't come back. Hours pass, then days. A rumor runs through the camp: 'Uthman has been killed. A camp of pilgrims, far from home, armed only for travel, gathered by a tree. And the Prophet asks each of them for a pledge.

Verse eighteen of Surah Al-Fath, in Pickthall's translation: "Allah was well pleased with the believers when they swore allegiance unto thee beneath the tree." The verse goes on: He knew what was in their hearts, and sent down peace of reassurance on them, and rewarded them with a near victory. The pledge is called Bay'at ar-Ridwan, the Pledge of Good Pleasure, after the word in the verse: Allah was pleased. Bay'ah is a pledge sealed with the hand, the root of buying and selling, a deal struck palm to palm. One by one they came and placed their hand in his. The hadith reports say they pledged to stand firm and not to flee. Then a detail the hadith keeps. 'Uthman wasn't there to pledge. So the Prophet held up his own right hand and said this is the hand of 'Uthman, and struck it on his left, pledging on his absent friend's behalf. As it turned out, 'Uthman was alive; he'd been held in Mecca. And the tree? A report in Sahih al-Bukhari says that the next year, some who had been there could not find it again. Later reports, outside Bukhari, say 'Umar had a tree cut down when people began to visit it to pray, so that the place would not become a shrine. Either way, the tree is gone. What lasts is the verse, and the people it names. The verse names them as people with whom Allah was pleased, and they are remembered as the people of the tree. The pledge mattered not because the moment was safe, but because it wasn't.
screen: `BAY'AT AR-RIDWAN: ALLAH WAS PLEASED.` · `BAY'AH: A HAND IN A HAND.` · `THIS IS THE HAND OF 'UTHMAN.` · `THE TREE IS GONE; THE VERSE REMAINS.`

segments.voice: The practice: renew a commitment. Sit, and rest your right hand on your left. Think of a promise you made that matters: to a person, to your faith, to yourself, a vow at a wedding, a promise to a child, a promise to show up. Picture the moment you first made it. Then, quietly, make it again, in the present tense. If you pray, you can ask for help keeping it. The bell holds the time.
Bay'ah: a pledge sealed with the hand, the deal struck palm to palm beneath the tree at Hudaybiyyah. Today's word.
Your line: pledged under the tree. Today, keep one promise a little better than you need to: arrive early, call back, finish it fully. Day five hundred eighty-two.

583.title: Lower your voices
583.hook: don't raise your voices above the Prophet's voice (49:2)
583.howItsDone: Muslims are taught to speak quietly in mosques, and visitors to the Prophet's mosque in Medina recall this verse at his grave; scholars also apply it to how hadith and his teaching are discussed.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bay'ah, the promise made hand in hand when the moment wasn't safe. Your line was pledged under the tree. Which promise did you keep a little better? Day five hundred eighty-three.

Two people talking over each other, then three, each a little louder, until nobody is listening and everyone is shouting a point at the ceiling. Usually it's an office or a family dinner. Once, the reports say, it happened in Medina, in front of the Prophet ﷺ, and the two rising voices belonged to Abu Bakr and 'Umar. That scene sits behind Surah Al-Hujurat, the Private Rooms, the forty-ninth surah. It's a short surah, and it reads like a manual for how a community talks.

Verse two, in Pickthall's translation: "O ye who believe! Lift not up your voices above the voice of the Prophet, nor shout when speaking to him as ye shout one to another." Then it adds a warning: lest your works be rendered vain while you don't notice. A report in Sahih al-Bukhari describes the occasion. A delegation came from the tribe of Banu Tamim, and Abu Bakr and 'Umar disagreed about who should be appointed over them. They argued in front of the Prophet until their voices rose. After this verse, the report says, 'Umar spoke to the Prophet so softly that he sometimes had to be asked to repeat himself. Another Companion took it even harder. Thabit ibn Qays had a naturally loud voice; he was the speaker for the Ansar. When the verse came down he stayed home, convinced his deeds were wasted. The Prophet noticed he was missing, sent someone to ask, and sent back a message: Thabit was not among the people of the fire, but of paradise. The surah's next verse praises those who lower their voices in his presence. Commentators extend the courtesy beyond his lifetime: to raise one's voice over his words, his teaching, is a related kind of disrespect. You may remember Luqman's advice to his son, earlier this year: walk modestly and lower your voice. Two surahs, two settings, the same instinct. Volume isn't the same as truth. Often it's a sign that listening has stopped.
screen: `LIFT NOT UP YOUR VOICES.` · `ABU BAKR AND 'UMAR, ARGUING.` · `THABIT, LOUD BY NATURE, STAYED HOME.` · `VOLUME ISN'T TRUTH.`

segments.voice: The practice: speak softly in a gathering. Sit, and breathe. Picture the next room you'll be in with other people: a dinner table, a meeting, a group chat that has a voice of its own. Choose one moment there where you'll lower your volume on purpose, especially if you disagree. Let your breath be slow and low now, so your body remembers it. If you pray, you can ask for a humble voice. The bell holds the time.
Abu Bakr. His voice, raised with 'Umar's in front of the Prophet, became the reason this verse came down, and he learned to speak so softly he had to repeat himself. Today's word.
Your line: the humble voice. Today, the next time you feel your volume rise in a disagreement, drop it by half and see what happens to the room. Day five hundred eighty-three.

584.title: Verify the news
584.hook: if a wrongdoer brings news, verify it, lest you harm people unknowingly (49:6)
584.howItsDone: Islamic scholarship built whole sciences on checking reports, above all the study of hadith chains and narrators; Muslim teachers today cite 49:6 when urging people to check news before sharing it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Abu Bakr's raised voice, and your line was the humble voice. Did you drop your volume in a disagreement, and what happened to the room? Day five hundred eighty-four.

A screenshot arrives in the family group chat. Something outrageous someone supposedly said. Within ten minutes it's been forwarded to three other groups, two aunts are furious, and nobody has asked the obvious question: is it real? The forward button is new. The problem isn't. In Medina, the commentators say, one unchecked account nearly sent armed men against a whole tribe. The verse tied to that story is a short rule about news.

Verse six, in Pickthall's translation: "O ye who believe! If an evil-liver bring you tidings, verify it, lest ye smite some folk in ignorance and afterward repent of what ye did." Evil-liver is Pickthall's word for fasiq, someone known to cross the line, whose word can't simply be trusted. Tidings is naba', not idle talk but news that carries weight, news people act on. And the command is one word in Arabic: fatabayyanu. Make it clear. Find out. The commentators tell the story most often linked to the verse. The Prophet ﷺ sent a man named al-Walid ibn 'Uqbah to collect the zakat from the tribe of Banu al-Mustaliq. He turned back before reaching them and reported that they had refused to pay and meant to kill him. Anger rose in Medina, and in the version in Musnad Ahmad a party set out toward the tribe. On the way it met the tribe's chief, al-Harith ibn Dirar, coming the other way, puzzled that no collector had arrived. They had gathered the zakat and were waiting. The report was false. Commentators differ on the details, and some question parts of the account, but the shape is what the verse addresses. Notice the reason the verse gives. Not just that lying is wrong. That you will harm people in ignorance, and then you'll be sorry. It's a verse about the listener's responsibility, not only the speaker's. One more detail: in one of the recognized readings of the Qur'an, the same word is recited fatathabbatu, make sure, stand firm before acting. Two readings, one instruction: slow down before you strike.
screen: `FATABAYYANU: MAKE IT CLEAR.` · `NABA': NEWS PEOPLE ACT ON.` · `A FALSE REPORT ABOUT A WHOLE TRIBE.` · `THE LISTENER IS RESPONSIBLE TOO.`

segments.voice: The practice: check a story before sharing. Sit, and breathe. Think back over the last week: was there something you passed on, out loud or with a forward, that you never checked? Don't scold yourself. Just notice it. Then set a small rule for the next week, maybe: no forward without one question first. Who said this, and how do they know? If you pray, you can ask for a careful tongue. The bell holds the time.
Fatabayyanu: make it clear before you act, lest you harm people in ignorance, from 49:6. Today's word.
Your line: verify first. Today, before you share one piece of news, about a person or about the world, check it at the source. Day five hundred eighty-four.

585.title: Make peace between them
585.hook: believers are brothers, so make peace between your brothers (49:9–10)
585.carry: repair with fairness, so the thing can hold
585.howItsDone: In Muslim communities, elders, imams and family members act as go-betweens to reconcile quarrels, often citing 49:10 and the hadith that setting things right between people outranks voluntary worship.

segments.voice: Yesterday, fatabayyanu, and your line was verify first. Did you check one story at its source before passing it on? Day five hundred eighty-five.

Some families have two people who don't speak. Two brothers after an inheritance. Two sisters after a wedding. Two old friends after one sentence nobody can take back. And around them, everyone else learns the choreography: separate invitations, careful seating, nobody mentioning the other's name. Years can go by like that. It's easy to decide it isn't your business. Surah Al-Hujurat says otherwise. It makes the people standing around the quarrel responsible for ending it.

Verse nine begins with the hardest case: two groups of believers actually fighting. Make peace between them, it says, and if one keeps transgressing, stand against that one until it returns, and then make peace with justice, and be fair. Then verse ten, in Pickthall's translation: "The believers are naught else than brothers. Therefor make peace between your brethren and observe your duty to Allah that haply ye may obtain mercy." Brothers here is ikhwah, and some commentators note that this is the plural used for brothers by birth: the family word. And the command, aslihu, comes from the root s-l-h, to set right, to repair. Islah is mending, the way you'd mend a torn thing so it can be used again. Notice that peace here isn't passive. It's not staying out of it. It's work, and it's assigned to bystanders. A hadith in the collections of Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi makes the point sharply. The Prophet ﷺ asked his Companions: shall I tell you of something better in rank than voluntary fasting, prayer and charity? They said yes. He said: setting things right between people. Because, he went on, ruining relations between people is the shaver, the thing that shaves away faith. Another hadith, in Bukhari, says that the one who makes peace between people, passing on good or saying good, is not a liar. The tradition gives the peacemaker room. Verse nine also insists on justice: making peace isn't pretending nobody was wronged. It's repair with fairness, so the thing can hold.
screen: `MAKE PEACE, WITH JUSTICE.` · `IKHWAH: THE FAMILY WORD.` · `ISLAH: MENDING A TORN THING.` · `BETTER THAN EXTRA FASTING AND PRAYER.`

segments.voice: The practice: help two people reconcile. Sit, and breathe. Bring to mind two people you know who are at odds. Not a war you can't touch: something close, small enough to reach. Picture each of their faces. Think of one true, kind thing each has said or could say about the other. That's the material a peacemaker works with. Decide on one small step: a message, an invitation, a softer word passed along. If you pray, you can pray for them both. The bell holds the time.
Islah: mending, setting right, assigned by 49:10 to the people standing around a quarrel. Today's word.
Your line: repair with fairness, so the thing can hold. Today, carry one kind word from one person to another who needs to hear it. Day five hundred eighty-five.

586.title: No mocking, no nicknames
586.hook: don't mock others, they may be better than you, and don't insult with names (49:11)
586.howItsDone: Muslim scholars count mocking and hurtful nicknames among the sins of the tongue; affectionate names a person welcomes, like Abu Hurayrah, are accepted, while names someone dislikes are avoided.

segments.voice: Yesterday, make peace between them: islah, mending, the work the verse gives to bystanders. Your line was repair with fairness, so the thing can hold. Whose kind word did you carry? Day five hundred eighty-six.
screen: `REPAIR WITH FAIRNESS, SO THE THING CAN HOLD.`

segments.voice: Almost everyone had one. The nickname from middle school that started as a joke about your ears, your name, your accent, your weight, and followed you for years. Some people laugh about theirs now. Some still flinch when they hear it. The people who gave them out mostly forgot within a week. Surah Al-Hujurat, the surah of how a community talks, spends a whole verse on this, and the reason it gives is not the one you'd expect.

Verse eleven, in Pickthall's translation: "O ye who believe! Let not a folk deride a folk who may be better than they (are), nor let women (deride) women who may be better than they are; neither defame one another, nor insult one another by nicknames." Three things are named. Mocking, sakhar: laughing at someone to make them small. Defaming, lamz: the little digs, the jab disguised as a joke. And insulting with nicknames, tanabuz bil-alqab: the label that sticks. And look at the reason the verse gives. Not that mocking is rude. That the one you mock may be better than you. You can see a person's ears or accent. You can't see their standing with God. The mockery assumes a ranking the mocker has no access to. A report in Sunan Abi Dawud gives the setting. A man from the Banu Salamah said the verse came down about them. When the Prophet ﷺ arrived in Medina, many men had two or three names, and when he called someone by one of them, people would say: Messenger of God, that one makes him angry. So the verse was revealed. Notice the detail: the Prophet himself didn't know which names stung. Nicknames aren't always cruel. Many Companions carried names they loved: Abu Hurayrah, father of the little cat. The line the scholars draw is the one the verse draws: whether the name is one the person dislikes. A hadith in Sahih Muslim sums it up: it is evil enough for a person to look down on his brother.
screen: `MOCKING, DIGS, AND LABELS THAT STICK.` · `THEY MAY BE BETTER THAN YOU.` · `NAMES THAT MADE SOMEONE ANGRY.` · `ABU HURAYRAH LOVED HIS.`

segments.voice: The practice: stop one nickname. Sit, and breathe. Think of the names you use for people, out loud or in your head: a coworker, a sibling, a politician, a driver who cut you off. Find one that's really a small insult. Picture that person hearing it. Then decide to drop it, starting today, and choose their real name instead. If you were given a name that still stings, you can also let yourself set it down. If you pray, you can pray for them. The bell holds the time.
No mocking. The rule of 49:11: no deriding, no digs, no hurtful nicknames, because the one you mock may be better than you. Today's word.
Your line: they may be better. Today, when you're tempted to laugh at someone, remind yourself you can't see their whole story, and say their real name. Day five hundred eighty-six.

587.title: Suspicion, spying, backbiting
587.hook: avoid much suspicion, don't spy, don't backbite, like eating your dead brother's flesh (49:12)
587.howItsDone: Muslim scholars count ghibah among the major sins of the tongue; they teach that when you hear backbiting you should defend the absent person or leave, and that someone you've backbitten should be prayed for or asked for forgiveness.

segments.voice: Yesterday, no mocking, no nicknames, and your line was they may be better. Did you drop one label and use someone's real name? Day five hundred eighty-seven.

It usually starts small, and it takes no effort at all. Someone leaves the room, and the conversation shifts half a degree. Did you notice how she…? Has he always been like that? Nobody's lying. Everything said is true, or true enough. And it can feel pleasant, that warm feeling of being on the inside of a group that's outside someone else. Surah Al-Hujurat's twelfth verse answers that warm feeling with a hard, physical picture.
screen: `A HARD PICTURE FOR A WARM FEELING.`

segments.voice: Verse twelve moves in three steps, each closer to the mouth. Pickthall's translation: "O ye who believe! Shun much suspicion; for lo! some suspicion is a crime. And spy not, neither backbite one another. Would one of you love to eat the flesh of his dead brother? Ye abhor that." First, suspicion in the mind: zann, assuming the worst. Not all suspicion, but much of it, because some of it is sin. Second, spying, tajassus: going looking for what's hidden, checking someone's phone, digging for their faults. Third, ghibah, backbiting: saying it. And then the image. A dead brother, who can't defend himself, and you eating him. Commentators explain the image: the absent person is like the dead, present in the conversation, unable to answer. The verse doesn't explain the image. It just asks: would you love that? And answers for you: you'd hate it. A hadith in Sahih Muslim defines ghibah exactly. The Prophet ﷺ asked: do you know what backbiting is? They said Allah and His Messenger know best. He said: mentioning your brother with something he would dislike. Someone asked: what if what I say is true? He said: if it's true, you have backbitten him. If it's false, you have slandered him. That's the surprise. Ghibah is about the true things. Scholars do list exceptions, like seeking help against an injustice, or warning someone about a business partner or a marriage proposal, where the truth protects someone. But the default is clear, and the image leaves a simple test: would you say it with them in the room?
screen: `ZANN: ASSUMING THE WORST.` · `TAJASSUS: GOING LOOKING.` · `GHIBAH: SAYING IT.` · `TRUE, AND STILL BACKBITING.`

segments.voice: The outline's practice is a whole day without backbiting. Start here. Sit, and breathe. Picture the people you'll talk to today, and the people you're likely to talk about. For each absent person, imagine them sitting in the room, listening. What would you still say? Let that be today's limit. If you slip, don't spiral; just stop mid-sentence and change the subject. If you pray, you can ask forgiveness for the person you spoke about. The bell holds the time.
Ghibah. Backbiting: mentioning someone in their absence with something they'd dislike, even when it's true, pictured in 49:12 as eating a dead brother's flesh. Today's word.
Your line: not behind their back. Today, when a conversation turns to someone who isn't there, say one good thing about them, or change the subject. Day five hundred eighty-seven.

588.title: To know one another
588.hook: We made you nations and tribes to know one another, and the most honored is the most mindful (49:13)
588.carry: made different to know each other
588.howItsDone: Muslims cite 49:13 against racism and tribalism, and the farewell sermon's words on Arab and non-Arab, red and black, are read in Friday sermons and at the pilgrimage.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was ghibah, backbiting, true or not, and your line was not behind their back. When a conversation turned to someone absent, what did you do? Day five hundred eighty-eight, the end of the week.

Arabic, Urdu, Malay, Turkish, Swahili, Hausa, Bosnian, French, English with a Texas accent. During the pilgrimage, all of it rises from one courtyard in Mecca, from faces of every shade in the same white cloth. The Qur'an has a verse about why humanity comes in so many kinds. It's the thirteenth verse of Surah Al-Hujurat, and for once in this surah it isn't addressed to believers. It's addressed to everyone.

Notice the shift. Again and again, this surah has called out: O ye who believe. Verse thirteen opens wider. Pickthall's translation: "O mankind! Lo! We have created you male and female, and have made you nations and tribes that ye may know one another. Lo! the noblest of you, in the sight of Allah, is the best in conduct." Three moves. First, one origin: male and female, which commentators read as Adam and Hawwa, one family. Second, deliberate difference: nations and tribes, made, on purpose. Third, the purpose of that difference, in one Arabic word: li-ta'arafu, so that you may know one another. The form of the verb means mutual knowing, back and forth, each side learning the other. Its root is the same as ma'ruf, the known good, and 'urf, custom. Difference here isn't a problem to solve. It's an introduction. And then the ranking is taken away from everything you can see. The noblest is the most mindful; the Arabic is atqakum, from taqwa, the awareness of God. Not the richest, not the oldest family, not the right tribe. And taqwa can't be seen from outside. The verse leaves that judgment to the sight of Allah. A sermon attributed to the Prophet ﷺ during his farewell pilgrimage, recorded in the Musnad of Ahmad, put it plainly: no Arab has merit over a non-Arab, nor a non-Arab over an Arab, nor red over black, nor black over red, except by taqwa. This week has been the surah's whole lesson in talking well: a pledge, a lower voice, checked news, peace made, mocking dropped, backbiting refused. It ends here, with why the people across the table are different in the first place.

Taqwa: the awareness of God, the only thing by which 49:13 says anyone is more noble than another. Today's word.
Your line: made different to know each other. Today, ask one person from a different background one real question, and listen to the whole answer. Day five hundred eighty-eight.
